problem: Indoor-trained RL PointNav policies fail at long-range outdoor navigation because they beeline toward the goal and get stuck on obstacles. Classical planners on outdated or inaccurate maps miss real openings, and prior outdoor learning methods rely on large real-world datasets.
motivation: Outdoor legged navigation covers hundreds of meters, where wrong turns and backtracking are costly, and outdoor simulators are hard to build. The paper asks whether a policy trained only on short-range indoor sim can transfer zero-shot outdoors if it gets a rough, inaccurate high-level map as a hint, with onboard depth handling local obstacles.
key_idea: Train a depth-based PointNav policy in indoor sim with an additional rough top-down occupancy Context-Map input (a human sketch or satellite/digital-map segmentation outdoors), plus a few sim2real tricks, to get zero-shot long-range outdoor navigation on Spot.
insight: The map acts as a soft hint rather than a plan, and the policy fuses it with depth. Real-world runs show that RRT* on the same map missed the bush opening, while the Context-Map policy reached the goal 3/3 times on every route. In sim, the policy degrades gracefully with noisy maps and regresses to No-Context performance with a blank map (79.8 vs 78.7 SR), whereas Context-Waypoint and Context-Trajectory policies collapse under noise (Context-Waypoint drops to 36.7 SR at 1.0m shift). Training with noisy maps makes it even more robust.
method: Context-Map input: a 2x100x100 top-down map (channel 1 is the binary occupancy map, channel 2 marks the agent and goal), rotated to the robot heading and encoded by ResNet18 into 512-d features.

Oracle context variants: Context-Trajectory (A* shortest path drawn on the map) and Context-Waypoint (next waypoint within 1m along the shortest path, as polar coordinates through an MLP), used as upper bounds.

Policy architecture: a 3-layer CNN on depth, goal-vector and previous-action encoders, and GRU 1. Scaled dot-product attention between depth and context features feeds GRU 2, which outputs a Gaussian over (v_x, omega).

Training: DD-PPO for 500M steps in Habitat on HM3D and Gibson (episodes up to 30m, avg ~8m), with kinematic control at 2Hz. The reward has geodesic progress, success 10, slack -0.002, backward -0.3 and collision -0.003 terms.

Transfer techniques: log-normalized goal distance for long-range goals, camera pitch randomization of ±30° for slopes, depth completion of real Spot depth (Ku et al.), truncation at 3.5m, and Random Erasing on depth during training.
Real-world context-maps: human sketches over Google satellite images, or auto-segmented OpenStreetMap roads/buildings.

setting.backbone: CNN + ResNet18 + attention + 2 GRUs policy (trained from scratch with DD-PPO)
setting.training_data: Simulated indoor episodes on HM3D + Gibson (~1000 scans), avg 8m and up to 30m; no real-world or outdoor data
setting.observation: Egocentric depth (Spot front cameras) + goal vector via egomotion/BD localization + top-down Context-Map
setting.action_space: Continuous linear/angular velocity (±0.5 m/s, ±0.3 rad/s) executed by the BD low-level controller
setting.privileged: none at test time (the Context-Map is a human sketch; the oracle waypoint/trajectory variants are sim-only upper bounds)

numbers.eval_set_note: 1200 indoor episodes from HM3D and Gibson scenes (from Kin2Dyn), mean over 3 seeds
numbers.extra: trained with perfect maps, evaluated with clean maps
numbers.evidence: Table hm3d_val row 2: Context Map 95.4±0.2 SR, 81.0±2.4 SPL

numbers.method: Context-Map with 50% cutout noise at eval

numbers.extra: human-sketched map; BD localization; BD obstacle avoidance disabled

numbers_note: No standard benchmark is used. Real-world SPL is not reported. Only the noisy-map results from the main text are listed.
results: In real-world outdoor tests on 3 routes (up to ~100m+), the Context-Map policy succeeded 100% with no collisions, while the No-Context policy got 0% and RRT*+Context-Waypoint missed the bush opening. In sim, the Context-Map policy beats No-Context by +16.7 SR (95.4 vs 78.7) and +24.6 SPL and nearly matches oracle context.
limitations: Depth and map can both indicate free space in front of thin obstacles (railings, glass), and depth range is only ~3m, so the robot cannot discover much better routes than the map hint.
Relies on BD localization, which may drift over longer distances, and needs a human-provided or auto-generated map.
Evaluation is small: 3 real routes with 3 runs each, and SPL is not measured outdoors.
